lead: Diesel smoke is the visible part of particles born in the fuel-rich core of the spray. There the fuel has far more fuel than oxygen, so it cracks into carbon-rich pieces that grow into tiny spheres and chains. Most of this soot burns later in the stroke; what survives, with oil, unburnt fuel and sulphate stuck to it, is particulate matter (PM). This chapter defines PM, follows a particle from birth to tailpipe, and shows how PM is weighed and why it trades against NOx.
prereq: You need: diesel combustion and its stages (Combustion in SI and CI engines), and the NOx route in formation of CO, HC and NOx.

blocks.text: Particulate matter is defined by the way it is measured: everything that collects on a filter when exhaust, diluted with clean air, is drawn through it at 47 °C. The filter is weighed before and after, and the gain is the PM mass. PM is a mixture of four parts:

items: Soot (dry carbon): the black solid core. It gives black smoke.
Soluble organic fraction (SOF): unburnt fuel and lubricating oil that condense on the soot as the gas cools. At light load it can be half the mass or more.
Sulphate with bound water: from sulphur in the fuel, burnt to SO2 and partly to sulphate. Low-sulphur diesel (10 ppm sulphur) has made this part small.
Ash: metal compounds from lubricant additives and engine wear, a few per cent of the mass. Ash never burns.

blocks.where: each term is a mass in the same filter sample, in mg; the water bound to the sulphate is counted with it.

blocks.text: Smoke is not the same as PM. You see black smoke because of the soot. A clear exhaust can still carry SOF and sulphate, and the visible colour tells the cause: black smoke is soot from too much fuel for the air; blue smoke is burning lubricating oil (worn rings or valve guides); white smoke is unburnt fuel droplets or water vapour, common on a cold start.

sections.h3: From rich core to tailpipe: six steps

blocks.text: In the core of a diesel spray the local equivalence ratio is far above 1, often 2 to 4, and the temperature is 1600 to 2600 K. Soot forms only in these hot, oxygen-poor places, and grows through six steps:

items: Pyrolysis: heat breaks fuel molecules into small pieces such as acetylene (C2H2) and builds ring molecules, the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH). No oxygen is involved.
Nucleation: PAH molecules stick together into the first particles, about 1 to 2 nm across.
Surface growth: acetylene adds to the particle surface; mass rises fast while the number of particles stays the same.
Coagulation: small particles collide and merge into larger spheres, about 10 to 30 nm.
Agglomeration: spheres stick into chains and clusters a few hundred nm long.
Oxidation: when the burning jet mixes with air, OH radicals and oxygen burn the soot. Most of the soot formed is burnt here; exhaust PM is what survives.

blocks.text: So engine-out PM depends on two rates: how much soot forms in the core, and how much burns out before the gas cools in expansion. Anything that leaves the late gas cool or short of oxygen lets more soot survive.

sections.h3: What moves PM, and the NOx–PM trade-off

blocks.text: These changes lower PM by shrinking the rich core or helping burn-out:

items: Higher injection pressure and smaller nozzle holes: finer droplets and faster mixing.
More swirl or a better bowl shape: faster air–fuel mixing.
Low-sulphur fuel and low oil consumption: less sulphate and SOF.
Higher load at the same air: more fuel per kilogram of air, a richer core.
Injection retard: lower peak temperature and less time for burn-out.
Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR): less oxygen and lower temperature for burn-out.

blocks.text: Retard and EGR are the two main NOx controls, which is the NOx–PM trade-off: the low temperature and low oxygen that stop NO forming also stop soot burning. A modern diesel escapes the trade-off by using EGR and retard for NOx and then trapping the extra soot in a particulate filter, or by moving to the low-temperature combustion of HCCI and RCCI.

examples.question: A 40 kW diesel engine has a raw exhaust flow of 0.05 m³/s at standard conditions. A partial-flow system dilutes a sample of the exhaust 8 times (1 part exhaust to 7 parts filtered air) and draws 0.30 m³ of the diluted gas through a filter at 47 °C. The filter gains 0.90 mg. Find the raw PM concentration, the PM mass flow and the brake-specific PM.
steps: Concentration on the filter (diluted): 0.90 mg ÷ 0.30 m³ = 3.0 mg/m³.
Undo the dilution: raw concentration = 3.0 × 8 = 24 mg/m³.
PM mass flow: 24 mg/m³ × 0.05 m³/s = 1.2 mg/s.
Compare with a heavy-engine limit of 0.01 g/kWh: a filter must catch 1 − 0.01/0.108 = 0.907, about 91 % of the mass.
examples.answer: Raw PM is 24 mg/m³, the PM flow 1.2 mg/s, and the brake-specific PM 0.108 g/kWh, so the engine needs a particulate filter of at least about 91 % efficiency to reach 0.01 g/kWh.

examples.question: An opacimeter with an effective light path of 0.430 m reads 45 % opacity during a free-acceleration test. Find the light absorption coefficient k, which in-use smoke limits use.
steps: Opacity N is the share of light blocked: transmitted fraction = 1 − 0.45 = 0.55.
Beer–Lambert law: transmitted fraction = e<sup>−kL</sup>, so k = −ln(1 − N) ÷ L.
examples.answer: k = 1.39 m⁻¹. The coefficient is used instead of opacity because it does not depend on the path length of the meter.

traps: Writing “smoke = particulate matter”. Smoke is the visible soot; PM also holds SOF, sulphate and ash, which can dominate at light load.
Treating the filter-sample volume as the engine’s exhaust flow. The filter sees diluted gas: multiply by the dilution ratio, then by the real exhaust flow.
Treating opacity, Bosch smoke number and filter smoke number as the same or as PM mass. They measure light extinction or paper blackening, mostly from soot, and use different scales.
Saying soot forms in the lean outer zone. It forms in the hot rich core and is burnt in the outer, oxygen-rich zone.
Assuming EGR always helps a diesel. It lowers NOx but raises PM.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of diesel particulate matter.
quiz.a: Soot (dry carbon), the soluble organic fraction (unburnt fuel and oil), sulphate with bound water, and ash.

quiz.q: Match the smoke colour to its cause: black, blue, white.
quiz.a: Black: soot from too much fuel for the air. Blue: burning lubricating oil. White: unburnt fuel droplets or water vapour, often at a cold start.

quiz.q: Why does soot form in the core of the spray and not in its lean edge?
quiz.a: The core is hot and oxygen-poor, so fuel cracks into carbon pieces that grow (pyrolysis and nucleation). The lean edge has oxygen and OH radicals, which burn the pieces instead.

quiz.q: Why can a low Bosch smoke number go with a high PM mass?
quiz.a: The paper blackening comes mainly from soot. At light load much of the PM is SOF and sulphate, which do not blacken the paper.

quiz.q: A filter gains 0.60 mg from 0.25 m³ of exhaust diluted 10 times. The raw exhaust flow is 0.04 m³/s and the power 30 kW. Find the brake-specific PM.
An opacimeter of path 0.430 m reads 30 % opacity. Find k.
Retarding injection lowers NOx but raises PM. Explain both from the same cause.
quiz.a: Later combustion lowers the peak burned-gas temperature, so less thermal NO forms. The same lower temperature, and the shorter time left before the gas cools in expansion, burn less of the soot, so more survives as PM.

beyond: Not for the exam. Particle number limits now count solid particles above 23 nm, and new rules move the cut-off to 10 nm because the smallest particles reach deepest into the lungs. Researchers watch soot form inside optical engines with laser-induced incandescence. Direct-injection petrol engines also make particles, which is why some now carry a gasoline particulate filter. Search next for “particle number counting”, “soot oxidation” and “diesel particulate filter regeneration”.

figure.caption: Top: the six steps from fuel in the rich core to the particle that leaves; the last step, oxidation, burns most of the soot formed. Bottom: the worked example’s sample. The filter sees exhaust diluted eight times, so its concentration is multiplied by 8 before it is applied to the whole exhaust flow.
